newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Audit of Guatemala ports won't affect shipments.
newsitem.headline: Audit of Guatemala ports won't affect shipments.

text.p: The appointment of government auditors to fight corruption in three Guatemalan ports and the suspension of port managers will not affect shipping, a government official said Monday.

"We assure exporters and importers that the ports are functioning normally. This is an internal measure that will not in any way affect port activity," Jorge Franco, deputy minister of communications and transportation, told Reuters.
The ministry made a surprise intervention Sunday at the Quetzal Port on the Pacific coast, Santo Tomas Port on the Caribbean Sea, and the General Administration of Civil Aviation in Guatemala City.
The ports of Quetzal and Santo Tomas each move 2.8 million metric tons of cargo yearly, a small majority of which is container cargo.

Franco said the port audits are directly related to the government's three-week-long purge of corrupt officials connected to a huge smuggling ring that cheated the government out of millions of dollars a month over more than 10 years.

In the purge, army generals and colonels, the deputy minister of the interior, the deputy minister of defense, police chiefs, a judge, prosecutors and other officials have all lost their jobs, suspected of contact with suspected smuggling boss Alfredo Moreno, who was arrested September 15.

Franco said it's not yet clear how much merchandise came through the ports without paying taxes and duties, but he said manual documentation of loading and unloading shipments made it very easy for merchandise to evade accounting systems.
"Everything is written on little pieces of paper. Sometimes you can't understand what is written. It gets lost a lot and it is subject to corruption," said the deputy minister.
According to Franco, the government will computerize information systems in the ports so that customs and the National Guard will get timely, correct information on cargo.
Franco said the boards of directors and managers at the three ports will remain suspended during the audits and auditors will take over administrative functions.
If investigations determine port officials were part of the corruption problem, they will lose their jobs, he said.
The audits will last "as long as it takes," said Franco.
